extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, editors, and anyone seeking guidance on clear English prose
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive rules and usage guidance for clear, concise, and correct English prose, covering principles of style (clarity, concision, emphasis, parallelism), matters of form (headings, numerals, quotations, references, syllabication, titles), and a long list of commonly misused words and expressions with corrections and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 13. Omit needless words.
rubrics_metrics.description: Vigorous writing is concise: a sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences; make every word tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make all sentences short, but remove unnecessary words/phrases. Revise common verbose expressions (e.g., 'the question as to whether' → 'whether'; 'there is no doubt but that' → 'no doubt'; 'used for fuel purposes' → 'used for fuel'; 'he is a man who' → 'he'). The phrase 'the fact that' should be avoided and revised ('owing to the fact that' → 'since', 'in spite of the fact that' → 'though'). Prefer positive statements and active voice over negatives and passive. Combine sentences that present a single complex idea instead of using a step-by-step chain (example contrasting a 51-word sequence with a 26-word combined sentence).

rubrics_metrics.name: 14. Avoid a succession of loose sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write paragraphs composed of many similar loose sentences linked by simple conjunctions (and, but, so) or non-restrictive relatives; such series become monotonous and tedious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you find a series of loose sentences of this kind, recast some: use simple sentences, semicolons, periodic sentences, or sentences of varied clause structure to remove monotony. Example shows a weak paragraph of several 'and'/'while' sentences contrasted to better prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15. Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form (parallel construction).
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of similar content and function should be outwardly similar; parallel form helps readers recognize likeness of content and function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary variation for its own sake. Ensure articles/prepositions applying to a series are used consistently (either only before the first term or before each term). Correlative constructions (both...and, not only...but also, either...or, first, second) should be followed by the same grammatical construction. Examples: 'Formerly, science was taught by the textbook method; now it is taught by the laboratory method.' Fix faulty series and reorder or recast long lists (or use tables) if many parallel items are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16. Keep related words together.
rubrics_metrics.description: Word order signals relationships; place words or groups that are related close together and separate unrelated elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long interruptions between subject and main verb by movable phrases; relative pronouns should follow their antecedents; modifiers should be next to the words they modify to avoid wrong relations (examples: 'All the members were not present' → 'Not all the members were present'; 'He only found two mistakes' → 'He found only two mistakes'). Exceptions: periodic sentences that deliberately interrupt order to create suspense; relative clauses and appositions may slightly alter usual order without harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: 17. In summaries, keep to one tense.
rubrics_metrics.description: When summarizing drama use present tense; for poems, stories, novels preferably present (past allowed). Whichever tense chosen, use it consistently; express antecedent action with perfect or past perfect accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If summary is present, earlier actions use the perfect; if past, use past perfect. Do not intersperse phrases like 'he said' repeatedly—indicate at start that it's a summary and then proceed. In critical/interpretive writing avoid mere summary; aim for orderly discussion with evidence. Example given for Romeo and Juliet summary in present tense.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18. Place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end.
rubrics_metrics.description: The most prominent element of a sentence usually belongs at the end; the end commonly hosts the logical predicate or new information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reorder sentences so the idea you wish to emphasize appears at the end; periodic sentences create emphasis by postponing the main statement. Beginning can also be emphatic (anything other than subject). The principle applies to words within sentences, sentences within paragraphs, and paragraphs within compositions. Examples show reordering for emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headings (matters of form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting rule for headings and manuscript pagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave a blank line after the title/heading. On succeeding pages, if using ruled paper, begin on the first line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals (matters of form)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to write dates and serial numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not spell out dates or other serial numbers; use figures or Roman notation as appropriate. Examples: 'August 9, 1918 (9 August 1918)', 'Rule 3', 'Chapter XII', '352nd Infantry'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses (matters of form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation rules for expressions in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sentence containing a parenthetical expression is punctuated outside the parentheses as if the parenthetical were absent; the expression within is punctuated as if it stood by itself, except omit final full stop unless it's a question or exclamation. If a wholly detached expression or sentence is parenthesized, the final stop comes before the closing parenthesis. Examples: 'I went to his house yesterday (my third attempt to see him), but he had left town.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations (matters of form)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to introduce and punctuate quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal documentary quotations are introduced by a colon and enclosed in quotation marks. Quotations in apposition or as direct objects are preceded by a comma and enclosed in quotation marks. Quotations of a line or more of verse begin on a fresh centered line and needn't have quotation marks. Quotations introduced by 'that' are indirect and not enclosed. Proverbial expressions and very familiar phrases need no quotes. Examples provided (Constitution provision, La Rochefoucauld, Aristotle, Wordsworth verse).

rubrics_metrics.name: References (matters of form)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to cite works and use abbreviations in scholarly writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviate frequently occurring titles; give full forms in an alphabetical list at the end. Prefer references in parenthesis or footnotes, not in the body. Omit words like act, scene, line, book, etc., unless referring by only one of them. Provide punctuated examples for plays, biblical citation, and classical works (e.g., 'In III.ii', 'IV.ii. 14', '_2 Samuel_ i:17-27').

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllabication (matters of form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for dividing words at line ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If some syllables fit at line end, divide the word unless only a single letter or two of a long word remain. Principles: (a) divide according to formation (know-ledge not knowl-edge), (b) divide 'on the vowel' (edi-ble), (c) divide between double letters unless at end of root (Apen-nines), (d) do not divide before final -ed if e is silent (treat-ed). Examples and treatment of consonant combinations provided. Students should examine syllable division in printed books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles (matters of form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting titles of literary works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly usage prefers italics with capitalized initials for literary titles. Usage varies by publisher; use italics (underscore in manuscript) except when writing for a periodical that follows another practice. Omit initial 'A' or 'The' from titles when placing possessive before them. Examples: The _Iliad_; _As You Like It_; Dickens's _Tale of Two Cities_.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words and expressions commonly misused — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A long list of frequently misused, redundant, archaic, colloquial, or hackneyed words and expressions that writers should avoid or correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: aim to express accurate, individual thought rather than rely on ready-made phrases. In many cases, recast the sentence instead of substituting word-for-word. The section contains many specific entries (see individual items) with corrections and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: All right.
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage note: 'All right' is idiomatic in familiar speech as a detached phrase meaning 'Agreed' or 'Go ahead'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In other uses better avoided. Always written as two words.

rubrics_metrics.name: As good or better than.
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct comparisons when using 'as good or better than'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rearrange sentence: 'My opinion is as good or better than his.' → 'My opinion is as good as his, or better (if not better).' Avoid awkward constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: As to whether.
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundancy: 'as to whether' is verbose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'whether' alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bid.
rubrics_metrics.description: Verb 'bid' takes the infinitive without 'to'; past tense meaning 'ordered' is 'bade'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct infinitive and past forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: But.
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnecessary after 'doubt' and 'help'; excessive use of 'but' leads to loose-sentence faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say 'I have no doubt that' not 'no doubt but that'; avoid stacking 'but' at sentence starts — reorder to avoid repetitive contrast. Example reordering: combine contrasts to avoid sentence-initial 'But'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Can.
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning distinction: 'can' = 'am/is/are able'; do not use it as a substitute for 'may'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'may' when permission is meant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case.
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'case' often redundant in the senses 'instance' or 'usual state'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more direct phrasing: 'Many of the rooms were poorly ventilated' (not 'In many cases, the rooms...'); 'Few mistakes have been made' (not 'It has rarely been the case that any mistake has been made').

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainly.
rubrics_metrics.description: Overuse: 'certainly' used indiscriminately as an intensifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous intensifiers; they're worse in writing than in speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Character' often redundant, used like 'nature'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'acts of a hostile character' with 'hostile acts' to be more direct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim, vb.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use distinctions: with object-noun, 'claim' means 'lay claim to'; with dependent clause it can mean 'assert'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't use 'claim' as substitute for 'declare', 'maintain', or 'charge' unnecessarily. Prefer 'claimed that he was...' sparingly; 'claimed to be' may be better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clever.
rubrics_metrics.description: Overused; best restricted to small displays of ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loose use; reserve for apt contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare (to/with).
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Compare to' points out resemblances between unlike orders; 'compare with' points out differences between like orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriately: life compared to a pilgrimage (to), Congress compared with Parliament (with).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider.
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'consider' means 'believe to be', it is not followed by 'as'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say 'I consider him thoroughly competent', not 'I consider him as...'. When it means 'examine', 'consider' can be followed by 'as' ('considered first as soldier...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Data.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Data' is plural (like phenomena, strata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plural verb: 'These data were tabulated.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependable.
rubrics_metrics.description: Often a needless substitute for 'reliable' or 'trustworthy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the simpler words unless nuance demands otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different than.
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorrect usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'different from', 'other than', or 'unlike' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divided into.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Divided into' differs from 'composed of'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'divided into' for plays (acts) but 'composed of' for poems (stanzas) — choose the correct verb for the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't.
rubrics_metrics.description: Contraction of 'do not'; distinguish contractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriately; 'don't' = 'do not', 'doesn't' = 'does not'. In formal writing prefer full forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due to.
rubrics_metrics.description: Misused as adverbial 'because of' or 'owing to'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'due to' when related as predicate or modifier to a noun (This invention is due to Edison; losses due to preventable fires). For adverbial use, substitute 'because of' or 'owing to'. Example: 'He lost the first game because of carelessness' (not 'due to carelessness').

rubrics_metrics.name: Folk.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Folk' is a collective noun equivalent to 'people'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use singular form only where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect.
rubrics_metrics.description: As noun, 'effect' = 'result'; as verb, 'to effect' = 'to bring about', 'accomplish'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse with 'affect' (to influence). Avoid vague uses of 'effect' in arts criticism ('an Oriental effect'); be specific instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Means 'and the rest' and should not be used when important particulars would be omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid after lists introduced by 'such as' or 'for example'. Acceptable when it represents the last terms of an already-complete list or innocuous trailing items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'fact' only for matters capable of direct verification, not for judgments of value or taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'the fact that' (see Rule 13). Examples: dates and measurable properties are facts; claims like 'Napoleon was the greatest' are judgments, not facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor.
rubrics_metrics.description: A hackneyed word that usually adds nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'factor' and rephrase: 'His superior training was the great factor in his winning the match.' → 'He won the match by being better trained.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature.
rubrics_metrics.description: Another overused word which often adds nothing specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace with concrete description of what is noteworthy (e.g., say what Miss A. sang rather than 'a feature... was the singing of Miss A.'). As a verb in advertising sense, avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix.
rubrics_metrics.description: Colloquial in American English for 'arrange', 'prepare', 'mend'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In writing restrict to literary senses like 'fasten' or 'make firm'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get.
rubrics_metrics.description: Colloquial 'have got' should not be used for 'have'; participle 'got' is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'have' rather than 'have got' in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: He is a man who.
rubrics_metrics.description: A common redundant and wordy construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elide: 'He is a man who is very ambitious.' → 'He is very ambitious.' Prefer to recast for concision: 'I have always wanted to visit Spain' instead of 'Spain is a country which I have always wanted to visit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Help (see under 'But').
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage note: similar issues as 'but' when following 'help'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'help' followed by an infinitive without -ing where structure calls for gerund: 'He could not help seeing that' vs incorrect 'help see'.

rubrics_metrics.name: However.
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'however' means 'nevertheless', it should not begin a sentence or clause; when it comes first it means 'in whatever way' or 'to whatever extent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place 'however' in the middle for 'nevertheless': 'The roads were almost impassable. At last, however, we succeeded...' If starting a sentence with 'However' the meaning is different (e.g., 'However you advise him...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Interesting.
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'interesting' as a perfunctory introduction; show the interest instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than announcing 'An interesting story is told of...', tell the story directly without the preface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kind of / Sort of.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Kind of' and 'sort of' have literal senses and informal hedging senses; avoid misuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict 'kind of' to literal senses ('Amber is a kind of fossil resin') and use 'rather' before adjectives when appropriate. Avoid informal 'kind of' meaning 'rather' in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Less' should not be misused for 'fewer'; 'less' refers to quantity, 'fewer' to number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say 'fewer men' not 'less men'; exceptions when a round number functions like a collective noun are noted ('less than a hundred'). Examples clarify distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Like.
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'like' for 'as' when introducing clauses; 'like' governs nouns/pronouns, 'as' introduces clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'as' before clauses: 'We spent the evening as in the old days', not 'like in the old days.' Use 'like' with nouns: 'He thought like me' → 'He thought as I did (like me)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line, along these lines.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Along these lines' and similar phrases are overworked and clichéd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer fresher phrasing ('to the same effect'). Avoid vague 'line' usages when more precise wording is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal, literally.
rubrics_metrics.description: Often incorrectly used to support exaggeration or violent metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve literal/literally for true literal meanings; use 'a flood of abuse' not 'a literal flood of abuse'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lose out.
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnecessary intensifier where 'lose' is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'lose out'; prefer 'lose'. Same applies to 'try out', 'win out', 'sign up' when simpler verbs suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most.
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'most' to mean 'almost'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'almost': 'Almost everybody' not 'Most everybody'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Nature' often redundant or vague when used like 'character'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more specific terms; 'Acts of a hostile nature' → 'Hostile acts'. Avoid vague 'lover of nature' without specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Near by.
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbial phrase 'near by' is not fully standard as adjective; 'near' or 'near at hand' preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'near' or 'near at hand' for adverbial use; use 'neighboring' as adjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oftentimes, ofttimes.
rubrics_metrics.description: Archaic forms; modern form is 'often'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'often'.

rubrics_metrics.name: One hundred and one.
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain 'and' in numbers like 'one hundred and one' in accordance with traditional English prose usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the 'and' in such expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: One of the most.
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid threadbare openings starting 'One of the most...'; they are clichéd and weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't begin paragraphs or essays with formulas like 'One of the most interesting developments...' Seek fresher openings. Also beware of subject-verb agreement errors in following relative clauses ('One of the ablest men that have...' not 'has').

rubrics_metrics.name: Participle for verbal noun (gerund possessive).
rubrics_metrics.description: Use possessive with gerunds when the actor is a noun; avoid ambiguity where the gerund functions as noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'Do you mind my asking a question?' over 'Do you mind me asking a question?'. Use possessive when it clarifies that the prospect is of the action not of the actor. When awkward, recast: 'If it should become necessary to reconsider the whole matter' instead of 'In the event of a reconsideration of the whole matter's becoming necessary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: People.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The people' is a political term distinct from 'the public'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse 'the people' with 'the public'; use the term appropriate to context.
